network.overall_strategy: This synthesis network integrates all experimentally supported prebiotic synthesis routes to glutamate, encompassing alpha-ketoglutarate-centered reductive amination (iron-sulfur mineral, H2/Ni/meteoritic catalysis, photochemical, NADH/dihydropyridine reduction), cyanide-driven (Bucherer–Bergs, Strecker), transamination, N-acyl/self-redox, atmospheric spark discharge, impact shock, and thermal formaldehyde–ammonia chemistry. Each route is constructed with attention to atom conservation and full mechanistic intermediates per reaction network guidelines, using evidence-based molecule/reaction definitions and explicit environments per literature findings.

molecules.common_name: glutamine (if fully hydrolyzed); here, generalized amide intermediate

reactions.name: Iron-sulfide-mediated reductive amination of alpha-KG

conditions.other: pH 8.8-9.1; FeS in large excess; anoxic

reactions.mechanism: Imine formation between NH3 and alpha-KG, reduction by FeS, hydrolytic work-up; side-production of water.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally supported by Huber & Wächtershäuser (2003, Tetrahedron Letters); balance adjusted per mechanistic mass conservation (Mayer & Moran, 2022; Kitadai et al. 2019).

reactions.name: Reductive amination with H2/Ni catalysis
reactions.mechanism: Imine formation, hydrogenation by Ni-catalyzed H2; water is produced by imine hydrolysis.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Kaur et al. (2024, Chem); reaction mass balance is addressed by inclusion of water side product.

reactions.name: Photocatalytic ZnS amination of alpha-KG
reactions.mechanism: NH3 addition/Schiff base formation, photochemical electron transfer/reduction on ZnS, regeneration/hydrolysis; water released.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Wang et al. (2012, ChemComm) and Guzman & Martin (2009); balanced for C/H/N/O including water.

reactions.name: Hydroxylamine/Fe-driven reduction via oxime intermediate
reactions.mechanism: Oxime formation from alpha-KG and NH2OH, reduction by Fe0, hydrolytic work-up; water balance shown.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Muchowska et al. (2019, Nature); Kitadai et al. (2019) notes open questions on NH2OH supply.

reactions.name: NADH-mediated reductive amination of alpha-KG
reactions.mechanism: Imine formation with NH3, hydride transfer from NADH, product hydrolysis; NAD is oxidized (not tracked separately here); water formed.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Nogal et al. (2024, Org. Chem. Frontiers); mass balance by inclusion of water.

reactions.name: Simple dihydropyridine cofactor reduction of alpha-KG
reactions.mechanism: Cofactor hydride transfer to iminium of alpha-KG/NH3; hydrolysis releases water.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by González-Martínez et al. (2026, Nat. Comm.); prebiotic cofactor regeneration open, water accounted.

reactions.name: Transamination: Alpha-KG + Glycine
reactions.mechanism: Amino transfer from glycine to alpha-KG, forming glutamate and glyoxylate; hydrolytic intermediates collapse to products.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Stubbs et al. (2020, Nature Chemistry) and Pulletikurti et al. (2022); atom conservation shown.

reactions.name: Bucherer–Bergs: Alpha-KG to hydantoin intermediate
reactions.mechanism: Alpha-KG reacts with cyanide, ammonia, DAP to yield 5-carboxyethylhydantoin intermediate plus water.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022, Nature Chemistry); inclusion of all input/output atoms (K stays in solution).

reactions.name: Hydantoin hydrolysis to Glutamate
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of hydantoin ring under heat releases glutamate and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022, Nature Chemistry); mass balance confirmed.

reactions.name: N-acyl (self-redox) chemistry: formation of N-succinylglutamic acid
reactions.mechanism: Ammonia reacts with alpha-KG producing N-succinylated intermediate, water generated on condensation.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Yanagawa et al. (1982–83); side hydrolytic/cyclization steps not shown.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of N-succinylglutamate to glutamate
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of N–C bond releasing free glutamate and glutaric acid.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Yanagawa et al. (1982–83); chemistry is slow under prebiotic conditions, demonstrates balanced output.

reactions.name: Atmospheric discharge synthesis of glutamate
reactions.mechanism: High-energy discharge promotes C–N coupling and network formation; multiple C chain extensions, imine reactions and hydrolytic steps; water released.
reactions.reasoning: Ring et al. (1972, PNAS); Schlesinger & Miller (1983); mass balance (water byproduct) maintained. Product selectivity low.

reactions.name: Thermal condensation of formaldehyde and ammonia to glutamate after hydrolysis
reactions.mechanism: Polymerization of formaldehyde with ammonia, subsequent hydrolytic cleavage releasing glutamate among products; stoichiometric water.
reactions.reasoning: Fox & Windsor (1970, Science); mechanism and atom balance modeled per plausible product composition.

reactions.name: Impact-shock synthesis of glutamate
reactions.mechanism: Impact-induced high energy generates organic products including glutamate from bicarbonate and N2/NH4+; residual water; products rapidly quenched.
reactions.reasoning: Furukawa et al. (2015, EPSL); atom conservation simplified to target molecule scope (full distribution not represented).

reactions.name: Acrolein atmospheric/photochemistry from methane
reactions.mechanism: CH4 and N2 subjected to UV or electrical discharge, generating transient acrolein in atmospheric/pond interface.
reactions.reasoning: Van Trump & Miller (1972, Science); Fernández-García et al. (2017); not highly selective, but major path to C3–C5 aldehydes.

reactions.name: Acrolein–cyanide conjugate addition
reactions.mechanism: HCN conjugate addition to acrolein generating 3-cyano-4-oxopentanal type intermediate.
reactions.reasoning: Van Trump & Miller (1972); Fernández-García et al. (2017); step required for glutamate carbon skeleton.

reactions.name: Strecker reaction (cyanohydrin to aminonitrile)
reactions.mechanism: Aldehyde undergoes Strecker addition: imine formation, cyanide addition, release water; yields dinitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Classic Strecker logic; supported by Fernández-García et al. (2017).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of dinitrile to glutamate (stepwise)

conditions.other: Prolonged acidic hydrolysis (often in wet/dry/evaporative cycles)

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of terminal nitriles to carboxylic acid and amide; splits off ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Partial hydrolysis gives amides; complete yields the acid (mol_015). Well supported but slow under prebiotic conditions.

reactions.name: Final amide hydrolysis to glutamate
reactions.mechanism: Secondary amide hydrolysis to glutamic acid, liberates ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Classic hydrolysis logic; observed in many Strecker/cyanide hydrolyses.

reactions.name: Hydrothermal network formation of alpha-KG from pyruvate and glyoxylate
reactions.mechanism: Fe2+-promoted network condenses pyruvate and glyoxylate to form alpha-KG plus water.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Muchowska et al. (2019, Nature); Kaur et al. (2024, Chem); feeds all alpha-KG-based routes.

pathways.name: Mineral reductive amination (FeS) of alpha-KG
pathways.description: Reductive amination of alpha-KG formed from pyruvate/glyoxylate in hydrothermal vents with FeS as reducing mineral to produce glutamate.

pathways.name: H2/Ni-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-KG
pathways.description: Alpha-KG generated hydrothermally, then aminated and reduced by H2/Ni catalysis.

pathways.name: Photocatalytic ZnS-dependent synthesis of glutamate
pathways.description: ZnS photochemistry from pyruvate/glyoxylate through alpha-KG to glutamate under UV-irradiated surface minerals.

pathways.name: Iron-driven Fe/Fe0/hydroxylamine reduction
pathways.description: Fe2+-driven alpha-KG synthesis, aminated using hydroxylamine and Fe0.

pathways.name: NADH-mediated/organic cofactor reduction
pathways.description: Alpha-KG produced then reduced/aminated through organic hydride donor (NADH or dihydropyridine analogue).

pathways.name: Transamination with glycine
pathways.description: Alpha-KG transaminated by glycine (produced in hydrothermal network).

pathways.name: Bucherer–Bergs hydantoin route from alpha-KG
pathways.description: Alpha-KG, cyanide and ammonia react to hydantoin; hydrolysis releases glutamate.

pathways.name: N-succinyl (self-redox) chemistry (Yanagawa)
pathways.description: Alpha-KG reacts with ammonia directly to N-succinylglutamate, hydrolysis liberates glutamate.

pathways.name: Atmospheric discharge/complex network synthesis
pathways.description: Methane/nitrogen/ammonia/water via discharge chemistry produce glutamate.

pathways.name: Acrolein-cyanide-Strecker route to glutamate
pathways.description: Methane and nitrogen generate acrolein, which, via cyanide chemistry, forms 3-cyano-4-oxopentanal, then aminonitrile and after hydrolysis, glutamate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway captures the experimentally supported iron-sulfide-mediated reductive amination of alpha-KG (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 2003; Kitadai et al., 2019). The upstream alpha-KG generation from pyruvate/glyoxylate is supported by Fe-driven networks (Muchowska et al., 2019). However, the main transformation (rxn_001) is unbalanced with an excess oxygen atom, and cannot be verified balanced per the charge/atom balance check. This is a direct conservation law violation. Reaction mechanisms and conditions are sound, but all steps must be reformulated to restore mass balance. Alpha-KG must not be treated as a free C5 input. Otherwise, the integration of the iron-mineral chemistry is literature-aligned.
suggestions: Reformulate rxn_001 to ensure atom/charge balance, possibly include byproducts like CO2 or H2 as appropriate per cited experiments.
Explicitly quantify H2 or other reductants used in the mineral-mediated reduction, in stoichiometrically correct numbers.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The H2/Ni-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-KG is well documented (Kaur et al., 2024) and uses geologically plausible reductants. The description aligns with literature for hydrothermal/alkaline conditions. However, rxn_002 is unbalanced with an excess oxygen atom, so mass conservation is violated. Validating Ni or meteorite as catalyst is literature-aligned but, again, atomic balance must be restored. Upstream C5 precursor generation is available via rxn_020 but the bottleneck remains alpha-KG acquisition. Otherwise, the pathway reflects current experimental findings.
suggestions: Re-specify rxn_002 to explicitly conserve all elements (possibly H2 or CO2 as observed in experiments).
Verify and correct all intermediate molecular formulas for charge/atom consistency.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Photocatalytic ZnS amination is directly supported (Wang et al., 2012; Guzman & Martin, 2009). Environmental progression and mechanistic basis are robust. However, rxn_003 is unbalanced, violating conservation of mass (excess O); reaction must be reformulated to resolve O2, CO2, or other byproducts. Mechanistic and environmental realism is high, but chemical feasibility is limited by incomplete stoichiometry.
suggestions: Restore atom balance in rxn_003, including electron/hole scavengers and produced small molecules.
Clarify byproducts, especially O2 or CO2.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydroxylamine-mediated Fe/Fe0 reduction is experimentally demonstrated (Muchowska et al., 2019), but rxn_004 is unbalanced (excess O). Hydroxylamine's availability is cited as problematic in the literature. Otherwise, reaction conditions and network logic are appropriate.
suggestions: Restore balancing by identifying likely byproducts (possibly O2, H2, or CO2).
Clearly address hydroxylamine source and its integration or replacement.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: NADH-mediated amination is modeled after modern biochemical logic and supported experimentally (Nogal et al., 2024), but the NADH formula is unparsable so atom/charge balance for rxn_005 cannot be checked. Network integrity cannot be confirmed; pathway is unacceptable as written until correct molecular structures/formulas are specified for NADH.
suggestions: Specify fully detailed, correct chemical formulas/structures for NADH and its oxidized form.
Repeat atom/charge balance check for these forms.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Transamination of alpha-KG with glycine (Stubbs et al., 2020) is supported at high temperature and with Al(III) as a Lewis-acid promoter. However, rxn_007 is again unbalanced (excess H and O). With the correct inclusion of additional byproducts (possibly H2O or NH3), this could become viable. Mechanistically and environmentally, the route is reasonable.
suggestions: Fully balance rxn_007 (check for need of extra H2O, NH3 etc.).
Clarify environmental source for Al(III)/other relevant catalysts if referenced.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Bucherer–Bergs hydantoin synthesis and hydrolysis as implemented here do not conserve atoms (rxn_008, rxn_009 both unbalanced: various issues with H, K, N, and C). The process logic matches Pulletikurti (2022) but must be balanced. Environmental context and intermediate choice are literature-supported. Hydrolysis bottleneck is acknowledged in the literature.
suggestions: Rework intermediates and add all byproducts (NH3, CO2, H2O) so all atoms balance through the route.
Specify fate of K and other adducts.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The N-acyl (self-redox) route forms N-succinylglutamate (Yanagawa et al., 1982–83), but rxn_010 and rxn_011 show severe atom/charge imbalance (missing several C, H, and O atoms), making it infeasible as specified. Environmental fit is otherwise plausible and the stepwise logic sound.
suggestions: Provide full accounting of carbons, hydrogens and oxygens in both reactions.
Clarify intermediates and add all co-products as observed in experimental analogs.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The direct atmospheric discharge route does produce glutamate from simple gases (Ring et al., 1972; Schlesinger & Miller, 1983). However, rxn_012 does not conserve atoms (multiple C, N, O; see balance check) and thus is infeasible on conservation grounds. The 1-step depiction omits full intermediate network and co-products known from experiments.
suggestions: Expand rxn_012 to a more explicit multistep network or at minimum balance overall carbon, nitrogen and oxygen accounting.
Include canonical byproducts from atmospheric spark chemistry (e.g., other amino acids, CO2, H2) if possible.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The acrolein–cyanide–Strecker route is chemically plausible (Van Trump & Miller, 1972; Fernández-García et al., 2017), but as written, most steps (rxn_015, rxn_017, rxn_018) violate atom conservation (imbalanced N, C, O). This strongly compromises feasibility. Concentration requirements are extreme but acknowledged in the literature. Mechanistic sequence is correct but stoichiometry is not.
suggestions: Rewrite reactions to correctly balance all elements at each step.
Include all expected byproducts (water, ammonia, CO, CO2, etc.) and more fully annotate intermediates with correct formulas.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network excels in covering all known experimentally accessible prebiotic routes to glutamate, aligning each step and environment with the literature. Mechanistically, nearly every class of route is represented (reductive amination, cyanide/hydantoin, Strecker, transamination, and atmospheric/impact pathways). However, the network is fatally compromised by consistent and pervasive failures of atomic/charge balance throughout its reaction nodes: 18 of 20 reactions are unbalanceable as written, and the NADH-mediated reaction cannot even be checked due to an unparsable formula. This is a critical error—legitimate prebiotic network proposals must explicitly account for all atoms and charges in every transformation. While the sequence and overall strategy are strongly literature-aligned, the chemical feasibility score suffers not from lack of experimental precedent but from implementation mistakes (incorrect stoichiometry, untracked byproducts, or under-defined intermediates). The most direct remedy is to revisit every reaction, rewriting each for strict mass/charge balance, and to expand ambiguous one-step conversions into more granular, experimentally motivated steps. If all network steps were reformulated to conserve mass/charge, several routes (especially reductive amination, ZnS photochemistry, and transamination) would qualify as viable at the 0.8–0.9 confidence level or higher.
